summary: Updates the meaning of the Control Flags field in the Layer2 Info Extended Community used for BGP VPLS NLRI as defined in RFC 4761. It updates RFC 4761 and is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: A tiny fix to how a few switches in a virtual network's message are read.

questions: what is the vpls control word
what does rfc 8614 change in rfc 4761
what happens on a vpls c-bit mismatch
subtitle: How BGP VPLS routers should behave when they disagree about control words and sequence numbers.

tldr.problem: RFC 4761 lets a router demand that peers use a control word (CW) and sequence numbers, but does not say what to do when a peer cannot, so a mismatched pseudowire simply does not come up.
tldr.mechanism: A C-bit mismatch no longer blocks the pseudowire: it comes up without the CW in either direction. An S-bit mismatch SHOULD still keep it down, though an override MAY be configured where there is no multihoming.
tldr.outcome: Networks that mix routers with and without CW support can still build VPLS pseudowires. The RFC updates RFC 4761 and is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 8614 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2019. It updates RFC 4761 and has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC.

sections.title: Introduction and Problem
sections.content:
RFC 4761 describes how BGP sets up a VPLS (Virtual Private LAN Service). In the BGP VPLS NLRI, a Provider Edge (PE) router uses Control Flags to say whether other PEs in the same VPLS should include a Control Word (CW) and sequence numbers in frames sent to it. These are the C-bits and S-bits.

The CW helps prevent misordering of IPv4 or IPv6 pseudowire traffic over Equal-Cost Multipath (ECMP) paths or Link Aggregation Group (LAG) bundles. RFC 4761 requires that when the advertising PE sets the C-bit and S-bit, the receiving PE MUST insert a CW and include sequence numbers. It says nothing about a mixed environment where some PEs cannot do this, and that is the gap RFC 8614 fills.
sections.plainLanguage: Some routers in a network can use a special numbered envelope and some cannot. The old rules did not say what to do when they met.

sections.title: Control Word (C-Bit) Behavior
sections.content:
A PE that sets the C-bit in its NLRI says it can send and receive frames with a CW. Under RFC 4761 the setting cannot be negotiated, and if the two ends of a pseudowire disagreed, the pseudowire did not come up.

  • If both ends set the C-bit, CWs MUST be used in both directions.
  • If both ends send a C-bit of 0, CWs MUST NOT be used.
  • If the ends disagree, CWs MUST NOT be used in either direction, but the pseudowire MUST NOT be prevented from coming up.

The last case is the change: the pseudowire now comes up without the CW.
sections.plainLanguage: If both want the special envelope, they use it. If only one wants it, they skip it and still talk.

sections.title: Sequence Flag (S-Bit) Behavior
sections.content:
A PE that sets the S-bit says it can set and process sequence numbers as described in RFC 4385. If both ends set the S-bit, non-zero sequence numbers MUST be used in both directions. If both send 0, sequence numbers MUST NOT be used.

If the ends disagree, the pseudowire SHOULD NOT come up. This avoids out-of-sequence ordering when several PEs multihome a site and advertise different S-bit values. Where a deployment is known not to use multihoming, an implementation MAY offer a user-configurable override that lets the pseudowire come up. In that case the PE advertising the S-bit as 0 should set sequence numbers in its frames to 0, and the receiver should not expect non-zero sequence numbers.
sections.plainLanguage: Numbering the pages matters more than the envelope, because mixed-up pages can confuse things. So by default, if they disagree, they do not connect.

sections.title: P2MP LSPs as Transport
sections.content:
BGP VPLS can run over point-to-point LSPs or over Point-to-Multipoint (P2MP) LSPs rooted at the PE that advertises the NLRI. When some PEs support the CW and others do not, a source PE that supports it should set up two P2MP LSPs: one carrying CW-marked frames to PEs that advertised the C-bit as 1, and one carrying frames without the CW to PEs that advertised 0.

The leaves of the two LSPs MUST NOT include any PE whose S-bit differs from the root PE's. Such PEs are on neither LSP. The ingress router should send separate NLRIs for the with-CW and without-CW cases.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender runs two delivery routes, one for receivers who want the envelope and one for those who do not. Receivers who disagree about page numbers get neither.

sections.title: Worked Example with Four PEs
sections.content:
The RFC's example has PE1, PE2 and PE3 enabled for CW and sequencing, and PE4 with neither. PE1 advertises C and S bits of 1. PE2 and PE3 send the CW and non-zero sequence numbers to PE1, while PE4 cannot. Under RFC 4761 the PW between PE1 and PE4 would not come up.

Under RFC 8614, PE1 still will not bring up the PW with PE4 because of the S-bit mismatch, unless local configuration on both overrides that. If PE4 instead advertised a C-bit of 0 and an S-bit of 1, the PW would come up despite the CW mismatch. PE1 would then strip the CW only from frames received from PE2 and PE3, and expect non-zero sequence numbers from all of them, including PE4.
sections.plainLanguage: One router cannot use envelopes or page numbers, so it is left out. If it could at least number pages, it could join without the envelope.

sections.title: Multihoming
sections.content:
In a multihomed setup, different PEs may represent the same service endpoint. For the C-bit, each PW SHOULD be evaluated independently: the PW between PE2 and PE1 could use the CW while the PE2-to-PE4 PW does not, because of a C-bit mismatch. Other multihoming behavior follows the VPLS multihoming work in progress.

For the S-bit, the S-bit rules of section 3.2 apply and evaluation SHOULD also be per PW. In the example, if PE4 does not set the S-bit, no PW forms between PE1 and PE4, so CE5 would effectively not be multihomed.
sections.plainLanguage: Each connection is judged on its own. One bad match can leave a customer with only one working connection instead of two.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security considerations of RFC 4761 apply. The RFC notes that bit-flipping media errors that cause a C-bit or S-bit mismatch do not adversely affect the availability of pseudowires under the new rules: they cause CWs not to be used, or the advertising PE not to expect non-zero sequenced frames. It says this is no worse than before, when such a mismatch kept the PW down. There are no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: If a flag gets garbled by accident, the worst case is that the special envelope is skipped.

viz.caption: WHAT HAPPENS WHEN THE TWO ENDS DISAGREE

cells: Comes up, CW not used in either direction
SHOULD NOT come up; override MAY be offered
